opus-5.5.text:
Oh, I love that website. It's very old-school: plain HTML, it looks like it hasn't changed much since the late nineties. There's no fancy design, no personal branding. It's just him.

What really appeals to me is that it's not only about research. Of course there are the papers, LeNet, convolutional networks, all the history. But there are also all these pages about his hobbies. He builds his own electronic wind instruments, he's into sailing and model airplanes, there's stuff about jazz, astrophotography, little gadgets he's hacked together. You get the sense of a person who is endlessly curious about how things work, not just someone optimizing for citations.

For me that was inspiring, especially as a student. Today a lot of academic pages feel like a polished CV or a marketing page. His feels like a personal notebook, a window into how a scientist actually lives and thinks. Research is just one expression of a broader curiosity about building things and understanding the world.

And honestly, there's something a bit rebellious about it too. He doesn't care whether it looks modern. He has strong opinions and puts them out there. That kind of independence, thinking for yourself and not following the trend, is something I really admire, and it's very consistent with how he does research.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, Yann's website — I think what I love about it is that it looks like it hasn't changed since the late nineties. It's this plain HTML page, no fancy design, and it's totally him. There's a stubbornness to it that I find charming. He's one of the most famous people in the field, he could have anyone build him something slick, and he just doesn't care. The content is what matters.

And honestly, that's kind of the appeal of Yann as a person too. When I was at FAIR, he was never trying to be polished. He would say what he actually thought, sometimes very bluntly, sometimes in ways that got him into trouble on Twitter. But you always knew where he stood. The website is the same — there's no marketing layer between you and his ideas. You go there and you find his old papers, his lecture notes, his opinions on where AI should go, and it's all just sitting there in Times New Roman.

I think for a lot of researchers of my generation, that page was actually a window into the field before deep learning became huge. You'd find the LeNet stuff, the energy-based model tutorials, and you'd realize this person had been working on the same core ideas for decades, through winters when nobody believed in it. So the site is a little bit of a monument to persistence. I'd never want him to update it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the website’s plain design and research materials, but does not mention jazz or French attitudes toward American popular culture.
